vignette:
He is 70 now, a widowed man from Latin America who has spent most of his life working with metal. Even in retirement, he still thinks like a welder: measuring twice, checking heat, trusting what can hold under pressure. He speaks in a steady voice at first, carefully and without drama, but his story comes in the order his body seems to remember it, beginning not with politics or ideology but with the room.

He is a young man when he is taken. He remembers the smell before anything else-urine, damp concrete, old sweat, something electrical burning. He has been picked up with others, questioned about people he knows, accused of helping men he barely recognizes. At first he believes there has been a mistake and that if he explains himself clearly, he will be released. Instead, he is blindfolded, shoved, stripped of time. In the room where they torture him, he loses the sense that words can protect him. He is beaten, shocked, held under water until his chest feels ready to split. He hears other men screaming and then grows afraid of his own voice when he hears himself join them. What stays with him most is not only the pain but the helplessness: the certainty that another person can decide whether he breathes.

When he is finally released, he returns home thinner, quieter, and older than he should be. His wife tries to touch him and he flinches before he can stop himself. He tells almost no one what happened. In his neighborhood, everyone knows enough to stay silent. He throws himself into welding because it is one place where fear can be controlled. Heat is dangerous, but it obeys rules. Metal distorts predictably. A torch in his hand feels different from electricity applied to his body by someone else. He becomes known as a careful worker, exacting, the kind of man who notices a weak seam before anyone else does.

But the past enters through small openings. The blue-white flash of the arc can pull him back without warning. If a coworker comes up behind him, his whole body jerks, and he spins around ready to defend himself before he recognizes where he is. He cannot tolerate having his hands restrained, even jokingly. He avoids basements, windowless rooms, government buildings. During storms, when power flickers, his stomach turns cold. At night he sleeps lightly, never fully surrendering. He wakes drenched in sweat, certain for a few seconds that he is back in that room. Sometimes he is ashamed to admit that at his age he still checks doors and windows more than once before bed.

His wife becomes the person who understands his rhythms without needing explanations. She learns that he prefers sitting near exits in restaurants, that he cannot watch films with prisons or interrogations, that certain smells can ruin an entire day. When their children are young, he is protective in a way that is loving but fierce. He scans crowds, keeps plans simple, insists on knowing who is coming and going. He calls it being responsible. His family mostly accepts this as part of who he is.

After his wife dies, the structure of his life collapses in a quieter way. Without her presence, evenings stretch too long. The apartment feels too still, and in the stillness memories get louder. He talks to fewer people. He stops taking small welding jobs because the noise and concentration exhaust him, and because there is no one at home to help settle him afterward. He sits in his kitchen with the television on low, not really watching. He startles at footsteps in the hallway. Some nights he keeps a light on because darkness feels too much like surrender.

He says he has spent decades "trying not to think," but now thoughts arrive uninvited. He sees the blindfold, the boots, the wet floor. He hears men crying out in voices that seem both strange and familiar. He feels anger that has nowhere to go-at the men who tortured him, at the years he lost to silence, at himself for surviving in a way that required becoming hard. He also carries guilt, though he struggles to explain it. He wonders why he came home when others did not. He wonders whether he said anything under torture that harmed someone else, even though he has no clear memory of doing so. His mind returns to these questions in circles that never close.

In conversation, he often minimizes. He says, "That was long ago," then grips the arms of the chair until his knuckles pale. He says he is "used to it," yet he has not slept through the night in years. He still studies every room he enters. He still mistrusts sudden kindness from authority. He still feels his chest tighten when he smells burned wiring. The young man in the interrogation room and the old man in the kitchen are, to him, not as far apart as they should be. Even now, he lives as though danger has only just stepped outside the door.
